part: 1

statements.quote: We can think of LLMs as machines that predict the next most likely word, given a context — only one word at a time.
That word is appended to the input and fed back in, and the loop repeats until a special `|endoftext|` token signals the end.
In the example below, the user enters the text “Once upon a” and lets the LLM continue.
🔄 The Autoregressive Loop: One Word at a Time Each word is appended and fed back in — the sentence builds one token at a time.
The aha It writes by reading itself.
There is no plan, no outline, no “dragon” stored anywhere.
Its output is appended to its input, the whole new text is fed back into the model, and the next word is predicted from that — again and again, until it writes the stop token .
But how does a string of words turn into a probability for the next one?
The machine has five steps.
Let us open it up and follow a single word through ↓
The LLM learned to predict the next word by reading **massive** amounts of text — books, websites, articles — noticing the patterns in how language works, and picking up facts along the way.

statements.quote: Computers don't understand words.
So the very first thing an LLM does is **chop the input into small pieces called tokens**.
We can first think of these tokens as words, but they don't have to be.
They can be sub-words, numbers, or any part of a text.
While we humans think in words, the LLM “thinks” in tokens.
Most tokens are common words or word fragments.
`"understanding"` might split into `"under"` + `"standing"` — two tokens.
That is the quiet genius of it: a word the model has never seen can still be assembled from pieces it knows by heart.
Where a word splits depends on the data the model was trained on.

It chooses that automatically, and once chosen, the vocabulary stays fixed for the life of the model — a fixedness with strange consequences for the rare tokens almost nobody ever trained on (\cite[Li et al., 2024]{glitchtokens}).
The aha It can read words it has never seen.
Break every unfamiliar word into familiar pieces and nothing is truly new.
The vocabulary never has to grow — is just + + , three pieces the model already knows.
✂️ Step 1: Tokenization — chopping text into pieces Type a word and watch it break into the pieces the model actually reads.
💡 Try typing “understanding” or “unbreakable” to see subword splitting in action.
The model breaks unknown words into known pieces it learned during training.
Spaces are tokens too — the ␣ chips are the whitespace between words.
+ A detour: tokens that break the machine open
Some tokens are almost never seen in training, so their embeddings stay nearly arbitrary.
Feed one to a model and it can spill nonsense or start reciting its training data — the “understanding” only reaches as far as the text it happened to read.
Researchers call them glitch tokens (\cite[Land & Bartolo, 2024]{land2024fishing}; \cite[Li et al., 2024]{glitchtokens}).
The most famous example is .
It is not a word and not a random string: it is the Reddit handle of a user who posted repeatedly in r/counting , a subreddit where people count upward, one number per comment.
Such names appeared so often in that corner of the web that the tokenizer gave some of them their own tokens.
But the vocabulary was built from a broader scrape of the web than the curated text used to train the model, so the model barely ever met them.
Ask it to repeat and it may answer “distribute”, refuse, or insult you.
Other counter names such as can make a model start reciting numbers (\cite[Rumbelow & Watkins, 2023]{rumbelow2023solidgold}).
That is the lesson in miniature.
A token is not a concept the model knows; it is a slot the model had to fill from data.
If the slot was filled with almost nothing, there is almost nothing behind it — and what comes out is whatever the surrounding statistics happen to drag along.
Go deeper Tokenization: How Words become Numbers
Next By itself, a number means nothing.
So how does “time” come to mean something — and “truth” come to mean something nearby?
Every token gets a place in space ↓
A raw token tells the model nothing about what a word *means*.
So the model replaces each token with a **long list of numbers** — a vector — that stands for its meaning.
These vectors live in a high-dimensional space where **words with similar meanings end up close together**.
To make this tangible, the demo below plots a tiny slice of that space — just two semantic axes the model might discover: **Power** and **Gender**.
“Man” and “Prince” sit close on the Power axis; “Man” and “Woman” sit close on the Gender axis.
Nobody hand-designs these positions.
The model learns them automatically during training, purely from seeing which words turn up in similar company across billions of sentences.
And the space doesn't just capture similarity — it captures **relationships**.
The direction from “Man” to “Woman” stands for the concept of gender.
Carry that same direction from “King” and you land right next to “Queen.” Nobody typed that rule in — it fell out of the statistics of the text (\cite[Word2Vec]{mikolov2013word2vec}).
Real networks don't use two dimensions but **thousands** — far too many to picture.
The principle stays the same: position encodes meaning, direction encodes relationship.
📍 Step 2: Embedding — Words as Points in Space
King − Man + Woman Man + Power Woman + 2·Power Prince + Power ↗ Directions
💡 Directions encode meaning.
The vector Man → Woman points in a direction that's the same wherever you take it — and so does Man → Prince .
The model was never taught this — it emerged from the texts themselves.
The aha Meaning became arithmetic.
Nobody told the model that Man → Woman is the same arrow as King → Queen .
The relationship simply is a direction in the space — and arithmetic on directions turns out to be arithmetic on ideas.
Go deeper Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
Next There is still a blind spot: to the model, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look exactly the same.
So how does order get back in?
“The dog bites man” means something very different from “The man bites dog.” Same words, different order.
So a **positional encoding** is added to each token's embedding — a unique signal that says “I'm the 1st word,” “I'm the 2nd word,” and so on.
Now each token carries two pieces of information: **what it is** and **where it is**.
This is not a nicety — the embedding and attention operations have no built-in notion of sequence order, so without it, the two sentences above would be indistinguishable to the model.
The aha Without it, word order does not exist.
Strip the positional signal out and “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” collapse into the identical, unordered bag of tokens — the same thing to the model, opposite things to you.
📐 Step 3: Positional Encoding — where am I in the sentence?
Each position gets its own wave-like fingerprint, added onto the token's vector.
Positional Encoding Heatmap
Same Word, Different Positions
Go deeper Positional Embeddings
Next Now every token knows what it is and where it is.
But not one of them has spoken to another yet.
Time to open the transformer ↓
This is the heart of the model — the **Transformer architecture** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}).
The token vectors flow through **many layers** stacked on top of each other (modern LLMs can have 80+ layers), each one refining the model's understanding a little more.
In general $\mathbf{h}_{l+1} = \mathbf{h}_{l} + \text{Layer}(\mathbf{h}_{l})$, starting from $\mathbf{h}_{0} = \mathbf{x}_{0}$.
This running vector is called the **residual stream**.

It was originally invented to prevent the **vanishing gradient problem**, but it also acts as a **shared notebook**: each layer reads from the notebook, does some thinking, and **writes its findings back** to it.
Attention lets the model **look at other tokens** to understand context.

statements.quote: After attention has gathered context, a small **neural network** processes each token on its own.
Unlike attention, it does not look at other tokens — it looks at one token's vector and transforms it.
In a modern LLM this block holds about **two-thirds of all the parameters**, which is why most of the model's stored knowledge lives here (\cite[Geva et al., 2021]{geva2021kv}).
The usual cartoon says three things happen: pattern detectors fire, a filter zeroes the weak ones, and knowledge is added back.
That is a useful first picture — but the modern version is sharper and a little stranger:
- **It is a key → value memory.** The first matrix holds thousands of *keys*: patterns in the token's vector.
When a key matches, the second matrix writes a *value* — not a stored sentence, but a **distribution over the next tokens** that this kind of pattern tends to be followed by.
Lower layers key on shallow patterns (word forms, syntax); upper layers key on meaning.
- **It is where facts are recalled.** In the middle layers the FFN behaves like an associative memory for subject → attribute facts.

Researchers can locate a single fact there and edit the weights to change it: the ROME method can make a model “believe” a different capital of France without retraining it (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022locating}).

- **The clean little cards are a convenient lie.** Real neurons are mostly *polysemantic* — one neuron responds to several unrelated things — because the model packs far more features than it has neurons, a phenomenon called superposition (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}).

Sparse autoencoders can untangle those activations into features a human can actually read (\cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}; \cite[Cunningham et al., 2023]{cunningham2023sparse}).

- **Modern FFNs are often gated, and sometimes replaced.** Many current models swap the hard ReLU for a gated activation such as SwiGLU, where one branch controls how much of another passes through (\cite[Shazeer, 2020]{shazeer2020glu}).
And because this block is so large, some models replace it with a **mixture of experts** — many FFNs, with each token routed to only a few of them (\cite[Fedus et al., 2022]{fedus2022switch}).
Let us follow the word **“Apple”**.
Thanks to attention, its vector already carries clues about its context.
Depending on whether those clues say *eating* or *buying*, a different set of keys matches — and a different value distribution is written into the stream.
🍎 Context: “eating an apple”
💻 Context: “buying an apple”
Values · next-token hints
Choose a context: the same word meets a different set of keys.
The aha The same word, two different meanings.
“Apple” is one vector, but a different set of keys matches depending on the company it keeps — and each key writes a different value: pie and juice, or Mac and iPhone.
The model did not look a fact up; a pattern matched, and a distribution over the next words shifted.
Go deeper Where 'Paris' Lives — How an LLM Retrieves a Fact
Technically, this is expressed with the formula:
The outputs of the attention heads, and then of the feed-forward network, are added straight back to the **residual stream** — nothing is overwritten, every layer only adds.
And crucially, neither the attention heads nor the feed-forward network are configured by hand.
They learn what to look for by looking at massive amounts of data.
Step 4: The Residual Stream — one shared notebook Step through the layers and watch the running representation build up, one write at a time.
The aha Nothing is ever overwritten.
Every layer reads the same running stream — “what the sentence means so far” — thinks for a moment, and writes its finding back, added on top.
Eighty layers deep, the original word is still in there.
The network is less a pipeline than one shared notebook , passed hand to hand and annotated by everyone.

statements.quote: After all the layers, the model takes the **last token's vector** and produces a **score for every word in its vocabulary** (often 50,000+ words).
Those scores are turned into probabilities:
Then it **picks a word** — usually one of the top candidates, but with a little randomness, so it doesn't say the exact same thing every time.
And then, as in the very first example, that word is appended to the input and the whole process begins again, one word at a time, until the model decides it is done.
🎯 Step 5: The Final Prediction — a probability over the whole vocabulary Input: “Once upon a” → what comes next?
Drag the temperature to change the model's mood.
🎲 Creative 1.00 (balanced)
💡 Temperature controls randomness.
At T→0 the model always picks the top word (greedy); at high T the distribution flattens and rare words get a chance — that is where LLM “creativity” comes from.
The model does not know the answer.
It assigns probabilities and samples .
A single prediction is one slice through a tube of plausible continuations.
Step through the sentence and watch the tube narrow as the context closes the options — then turn up the temperature and watch it inflate again.
The aha It does not know the answer.
The model never decides that something is right.
It builds a distribution over the entire vocabulary and draws from it — so the very thing we call creativity is a controlled amount of randomness in the draw.
Go deeper Temperature & Sampling
There is no “understanding” module, no grammar checker, no knowledge database.
It's all just vectors flowing through layers of simple math: addition, multiplication, and comparison.
But stack enough of these simple operations together, and something that *looks a lot like understanding* emerges.
The hypothesis that drives much of modern scaling research goes further: to compress natural language well, you must model the **causal structure of the world** that generates language.

statements.quote: A model thinks in a continuous space, yet it must speak in a **finite** vocabulary.

This meadow shows how a thought becomes a word: every word is a pin in the field, every point of the field is a possible next-thought, and the thought simply falls into the cell of the **nearest** word.
The seams between cells are exactly the places where two words are equally near — where language runs out.
> **In one line:** a language model is a finite vocabulary laid over an infinite space of meaning — and a loop that keeps falling from one point in that space to the next word.
The geometry of choosing a word Words are pins; each one owns the region of thoughts closest to it.
The line between two regions is a seam where the thought could tip either way.

The aha It writes by reading itself. There is no plan, no outline, no “dragon” stored anywhere. Its output is appended to its input, the whole new text is fed back into the model, and the next word is predicted from that — again and again, until it writes the stop token .
Still curious? Fine. But how does a string of words turn into a probability for the next one? The machine has five steps. Let us open it up and follow a single word through ↓
How does the computer find the next word?
blocks.section: How does the computer find the next word?

blocks.quote: The LLM learned to predict the next word by reading **massive** amounts of text — books, websites, articles — noticing the patterns in how language works, and picking up facts along the way. But how does it get from a string of words to a single prediction? It happens in five steps. We will follow one word through all of them.
blocks.section: How does the computer find the next word?

blocks.quote: Step 1: Tokenization

Computers don't understand words. They understand numbers. So the very first thing an LLM does is **chop the input into small pieces called tokens**. We can first think of these tokens as words, but they don't have to be. They can be sub-words, numbers, or any part of a text. While we humans think in words, the LLM “thinks” in tokens.

Most tokens are common words or word fragments. `"understanding"` might split into `"under"` + `"standing"` — two tokens. That is the quiet genius of it: a word the model has never seen can still be assembled from pieces it knows by heart.

Where a word splits depends on the data the model was trained on. It chooses that automatically, and once chosen, the vocabulary stays fixed for the life of the model — a fixedness with strange consequences for the rare tokens almost nobody ever trained on (\cite[Li et al., 2024]{glitchtokens}).

The aha It can read words it has never seen. Break every unfamiliar word into familiar pieces and nothing is truly new. The vocabulary never has to grow — is just + + , three pieces the model already knows.
✂️ Step 1: Tokenization — chopping text into pieces Type a word and watch it break into the pieces the model actually reads.

💡 Try typing “understanding” or “unbreakable” to see subword splitting in action. The model breaks unknown words into known pieces it learned during training. Spaces are tokens too — the ␣ chips are the whitespace between words.
+ A detour: tokens that break the machine open

Some tokens are almost never seen in training, so their embeddings stay nearly arbitrary. Feed one to a model and it can spill nonsense or start reciting its training data — the “understanding” only reaches as far as the text it happened to read. Researchers call them glitch tokens (\cite[Land & Bartolo, 2024]{land2024fishing}; \cite[Li et al., 2024]{glitchtokens}). The most famous example is . It is not a word and not a random string: it is the Reddit handle of a user who posted repeatedly in r/counting , a subreddit where people count upward, one number per comment. Such names appeared so often in that corner of the web that the tokenizer gave some of them their own tokens. But the vocabulary was built from a broader scrape of the web than the curated text used to train the model, so the model barely ever met them. Ask it to repeat and it may answer “distribute”, refuse, or insult you. Other counter names such as can make a model start reciting numbers (\cite[Rumbelow & Watkins, 2023]{rumbelow2023solidgold}). That is the lesson in miniature. A token is not a concept the model knows; it is a slot the model had to fill from data. If the slot was filled with almost nothing, there is almost nothing behind it — and what comes out is whatever the surrounding statistics happen to drag along.
Go deeper Tokenization: How Words become Numbers
Next By itself, a number means nothing. So how does “time” come to mean something — and “truth” come to mean something nearby? Every token gets a place in space ↓
Step 2: Embedding
A raw token tells the model nothing about what a word *means*. So the model replaces each token with a **long list of numbers** — a vector — that stands for its meaning.

These vectors live in a high-dimensional space where **words with similar meanings end up close together**. To make this tangible, the demo below plots a tiny slice of that space — just two semantic axes the model might discover: **Power** and **Gender**. “Man” and “Prince” sit close on the Power axis; “Man” and “Woman” sit close on the Gender axis. Nobody hand-designs these positions. The model learns them automatically during training, purely from seeing which words turn up in similar company across billions of sentences.
And the space doesn't just capture similarity — it captures **relationships**. The most famous example:

The direction from “Man” to “Woman” stands for the concept of gender. Carry that same direction from “King” and you land right next to “Queen.” Nobody typed that rule in — it fell out of the statistics of the text (\cite[Word2Vec]{mikolov2013word2vec}).
Real networks don't use two dimensions but **thousands** — far too many to picture. The principle stays the same: position encodes meaning, direction encodes relationship.
📍 Step 2: Embedding — Words as Points in Space
King − Man + Woman Man + Power Woman + 2·Power Prince + Power ↗ Directions

💡 Directions encode meaning. The vector Man → Woman points in a direction that's the same wherever you take it — and so does Man → Prince . The model was never taught this — it emerged from the texts themselves.

The aha Meaning became arithmetic. Nobody told the model that Man → Woman is the same arrow as King → Queen . The relationship simply is a direction in the space — and arithmetic on directions turns out to be arithmetic on ideas.
Go deeper Embeddings: The Geometry of Meaning
Next There is still a blind spot: to the model, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look exactly the same. So how does order get back in? ↓
Step 3: Positional Encoding

“The dog bites man” means something very different from “The man bites dog.” Same words, different order. So a **positional encoding** is added to each token's embedding — a unique signal that says “I'm the 1st word,” “I'm the 2nd word,” and so on.

Now each token carries two pieces of information: **what it is** and **where it is**. This is not a nicety — the embedding and attention operations have no built-in notion of sequence order, so without it, the two sentences above would be indistinguishable to the model.

The aha Without it, word order does not exist. Strip the positional signal out and “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” collapse into the identical, unordered bag of tokens — the same thing to the model, opposite things to you.

Step 4: The Transformer Layers

This is the heart of the model — the **Transformer architecture** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}). The token vectors flow through **many layers** stacked on top of each other (modern LLMs can have 80+ layers), each one refining the model's understanding a little more.
In general $\mathbf{h}_{l+1} = \mathbf{h}_{l} + \text{Layer}(\mathbf{h}_{l})$, starting from $\mathbf{h}_{0} = \mathbf{x}_{0}$.

This running vector is called the **residual stream**. It was originally invented to prevent the **vanishing gradient problem**, but it also acts as a **shared notebook**: each layer reads from the notebook, does some thinking, and **writes its findings back** to it.
4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for *this* word?”
blocks.section: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for *this* word?”

blocks.quote: Attention lets the model **look at other tokens** to understand context. In *“The cat sat on the mat because **it** was tired”*, what does “it” refer to? An **attention head** figures this out by comparing “it” to every other word and deciding that “it” is most related to “cat”.
blocks.section: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for *this* word?”

blocks.quote: Attention Heads solve what linguists call **Long Distance Dependencies**: a word at the beginning of a long text may influence the meaning of a word at the very end. Attention allows to find out which word attends to which other word over short or even very long texts, and it can do so over the whole **context length** of the LLM model.
blocks.section: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for *this* word?”

blocks.quote: It does so by moving the Embedding of a word in dependence of the context it's used in to a place called **contextualized Embedding** that looks not only at the word, but at the context the word is used in.
blocks.section: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for *this* word?”

blocks.quote: This is best exemplified when using words that have multiple meanings, like “bank”, which could be a **river bank**, or a **bank** where you put your **money**.

This is what **Attention** does: it looks at the context a word is used in, and moves the **Embedding** of a word in the **Embedding Space** to a point closer to its meaning in the context it's used in.

A head may look like it reacts to nouns or verbs while in reality it is just a pattern learned from statistics — not programmed to react to those words, and not "knowing" what they are (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}).

blocks.quote: The aha Context physically moves the word. “Bank” is not one fixed point. In the context of water it slides toward the river sense; in the context of money , toward finance. Attention does not care how far away the clue is — it reads the context and moves the vector wherever the context points.

blocks.quote: Next Attention has gathered the clues. So where does the model keep all the facts it is about to bring to bear? It looks inward, into the feed-forward network ↓
blocks.section: 4a: Attention - “Which other words matter for *this* word?”

blocks.quote: 4b: Feed-Forward Network - “What do I conclude?”

After attention has gathered context, a small **neural network** processes each token on its own. Unlike attention, it does not look at other tokens — it looks at one token's vector and transforms it. In a modern LLM this block holds about **two-thirds of all the parameters**, which is why most of the model's stored knowledge lives here (\cite[Geva et al., 2021]{geva2021kv}).

The usual cartoon says three things happen: pattern detectors fire, a filter zeroes the weak ones, and knowledge is added back. That is a useful first picture — but the modern version is sharper and a little stranger:

- **It is a key → value memory.** The first matrix holds thousands of *keys*: patterns in the token's vector. When a key matches, the second matrix writes a *value* — not a stored sentence, but a **distribution over the next tokens** that this kind of pattern tends to be followed by. Lower layers key on shallow patterns (word forms, syntax); upper layers key on meaning.

- **It is where facts are recalled.** In the middle layers the FFN behaves like an associative memory for subject → attribute facts. Researchers can locate a single fact there and edit the weights to change it: the ROME method can make a model “believe” a different capital of France without retraining it (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022locating}).

- **The clean little cards are a convenient lie.** Real neurons are mostly *polysemantic* — one neuron responds to several unrelated things — because the model packs far more features than it has neurons, a phenomenon called superposition (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}). Sparse autoencoders can untangle those activations into features a human can actually read (\cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}; \cite[Cunningham et al., 2023]{cunningham2023sparse}).

- **Modern FFNs are often gated, and sometimes replaced.** Many current models swap the hard ReLU for a gated activation such as SwiGLU, where one branch controls how much of another passes through (\cite[Shazeer, 2020]{shazeer2020glu}). And because this block is so large, some models replace it with a **mixture of experts** — many FFNs, with each token routed to only a few of them (\cite[Fedus et al., 2022]{fedus2022switch}).

Let us follow the word **“Apple”**. Thanks to attention, its vector already carries clues about its context. Depending on whether those clues say *eating* or *buying*, a different set of keys matches — and a different value distribution is written into the stream.

The outputs of the attention heads, and then of the feed-forward network, are added straight back to the **residual stream** — nothing is overwritten, every layer only adds.
And crucially, neither the attention heads nor the feed-forward network are configured by hand. They learn what to look for by looking at massive amounts of data.

blocks.section: 4d: A layer is a bend in space

blocks.quote: The residual stream shows *what* a layer writes. It leaves open *where* it writes it. Read the layer's output as a new coordinate system and the operation looks like a bend of the whole space: a smooth, reversible map that lifts the inside of a ring and lowers its outside, opening a gap for a flat classifier. This is the geometric picture behind the "origami" view of feed-forward layers \cite{keup2022origami} — except that here the bend is smooth, so no point is torn or glued. The hard ReLU crease is the subject of [Origami in N dimensions](origami.php).

blocks.quote: Step 5: The Final Prediction
After all the layers, the model takes the **last token's vector** and produces a **score for every word in its vocabulary** (often 50,000+ words). Those scores are turned into probabilities:

Then it **picks a word** — usually one of the top candidates, but with a little randomness, so it doesn't say the exact same thing every time. And then, as in the very first example, that word is appended to the input and the whole process begins again, one word at a time, until the model decides it is done.

The key insight

There is no “understanding” module, no grammar checker, no knowledge database. It's all just vectors flowing through layers of simple math: addition, multiplication, and comparison. But stack enough of these simple operations together, and something that *looks a lot like understanding* emerges.
Why next-token prediction is so powerful
blocks.section: Why next-token prediction is so powerful

blocks.quote: The hypothesis that drives much of modern scaling research goes further: to compress natural language well, you must model the **causal structure of the world** that generates language. When the training text says “I dropped the glass and it ___,” predicting “shattered” requires an implicit model of gravity, material properties, and causation. The model does not need to be explicitly taught physics; the compression objective pushes it to discover physical regularities because they reduce prediction error. This is the dominant interpretation of why scaling works: more parameters allow more compression, which requires more accurate world models, which produces more “intelligent” behavior. **From this perspective, intelligence and optimal compression go hand in hand** — intelligence is not a separate objective that has to be optimized directly.
blocks.section: Why next-token prediction is so powerful

blocks.quote: This framing is best read as a productive working hypothesis, not a proved identity. Solomonoff's theorem is a result about *prediction*, not about *understanding*: an optimal predictor must be a compressor, but it does not settle whether a *particular* predictor, including a modern LLM, has anything resembling genuine world knowledge — or whether fluent prediction can arise from large-scale surface pattern-matching alone, the position associated with \citeauthor{bender2021stochasticparrots}'s stochastic-parrots critique. The empirical evidence does not yet fully adjudicate the question; the practical success of scaling makes the compression-as-intelligence view hard to dismiss, but it remains a contested and deeply philosophical claim rather than a settled fact.
blocks.section: Why next-token prediction is so powerful

blocks.quote: The aha Prediction and compression are the same goal. To predict the next word well, a model has to find the shortest description of the data — and the shortest description of language keeps requiring a model of the world that produced it. Push prediction far enough and it presses into understanding.
blocks.section: Why next-token prediction is so powerful

blocks.quote: The Meadow of Words

A model thinks in a continuous space, yet it must speak in a **finite** vocabulary. This meadow shows how a thought becomes a word: every word is a pin in the field, every point of the field is a possible next-thought, and the thought simply falls into the cell of the **nearest** word. The seams between cells are exactly the places where two words are equally near — where language runs out.
> **In one line:** a language model is a finite vocabulary laid over an infinite space of meaning — and a loop that keeps falling from one point in that space to the next word.
